name: Agur
title: Author of Proverbs 30
summary: Agur, son of Jakeh, is the author behind Proverbs chapter 30, one of the most distinctive chapters in biblical wisdom literature. His background is unknown and debated – he may have been a non-Israelite sage from Massa, an area in northwestern Arabia associated with the descendants of Ishmael. The chapter begins with a moving confession of humility where Agur acknowledges human limitation before the Almighty God, followed by a powerful affirmation that God's word is pure and reliable. Central to the text is his famous prayer to be kept from falsehood and given neither wealth nor poverty – only the daily bread. Agur's use of numerical proverbs, drawing insight from nature's small creatures and the mysteries of creation, reveals a keen observer who unites reverence for God, intellectual humility, and deep wonder at the order of existence.

keyEvents.title: Agur's words of wisdom
keyEvents.description: Agur, son of Jakeh, presents his words of wisdom as a divinely inspired speech addressed to Ithiel and Ucal.

keyEvents.title: Humble confession of ignorance
keyEvents.description: Agur acknowledges his own limitations and asks rhetorical questions about God's incomprehensible greatness, with parallels to the questions God asks Job.

keyEvents.title: God's word is pure and reliable
keyEvents.description: Agur affirms that every word from God is refined and trustworthy, and warns against adding anything to God's word.

keyEvents.title: Prayer for honesty and self-control
keyEvents.description: Agur asks God to keep him from falsehood and give him neither poverty nor riches, but only the daily bread he needs – one of the most well-known personal prayers in wisdom literature.

keyEvents.title: Four Things That Are Too Wonderful
keyEvents.description: Agur uses numerical proverbs to describe four things that are too wonderful to understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a snake on a rock, the way of a ship on the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman.

keyEvents.title: Four Things That Are Small but Wise
keyEvents.description: Agur points to ants, hyraxes, locusts, and lizards as examples of small creatures with great wisdom, showing how nature teaches us about God's order.

keyEvents.title: Four Things That Move with Dignity
keyEvents.description: Agur concludes his numerical proverbs with four creatures that move with proud bearing: the lion, the rooster, the male goat, and a king leading his people.

versions.summary: Agur son of Jake is the author of Proverbs chapter 30. He is known for his words of wisdom and his humble reflections on God's greatness and human limitations. His words contain numerical proverbs and deep observations about nature and human life.
versions.title: The Wise Man from Proverbs
versions.reason: [minor] The title is clear, but could be slightly more specific, e.g., 'Author of Proverbs 30' to clarify his contribution.; [minor] The time period 'divided-kingdom' is a reasonable assumption based on the traditional association of Proverbs with Solomon's era and later collections, though Agur's exact dating remains unknown. Many scholars place the collection of Proverbs 30 in the post-divided kingdom period or even later. 'divided-kingdom' is acceptable given the uncertainty.; [minor] The summary is good but could mention that his identity and nationality are debated among scholars – some suggest he may have been a non-Israelite.; [minor] The sequence of events is slightly illogical: 'God's word is pure' (v.5-6) appears after 'Prayer for honesty and contentment' (v.7-9) in the list, but textually v.5-6 comes before v.7-9. The order should be adjusted so that the events follow the chronology of the text.; [minor] There is an unusual character in the word 'klippgrevlinger' – it appears to contain Cyrillic letters (пп) instead of the usual Latin 'pp'. It should be corrected to 'klippgrevlinger'.; [minor] The father is listed as 'jake'. The Hebrew name is 'Jakeh' (יָקֶה). The ID 'jake' may give the impression of a modern name. Check that this aligns with the system's ID conventions. The relationship itself is biblically correct.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Agur has several interesting aspects that should be covered: the linguistic interpretation of the names Itiel and Ukal, the question of Agur's nationality (possible connection to the Massa tribe), and the theological significance of the rhetorical questions in 30:4.

versions.summary: Agur, son of Jakeh, is the author of Proverbs chapter 30. His identity and origin are debated – he may have been a non-Israelite wise man from the region of Massa. He is known for his deep and humble reflections on God's greatness and human limitations, his famous prayer for honesty and contentment, and his numerical proverbs with sharp observations about nature and human life. His wisdom reveals a man who acknowledges his own ignorance before the Almighty God.
versions.title: Author of Proverbs 30
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is good, but the expression "the area of Massa" could usefully be refined slightly to "northwestern Arabia" to provide more context. Otherwise, it is well-phrased and theologically correct.; [minor] The chapter also contains numerical proverbs about four things that make the earth uneasy (v. 21–23) and four things that go with dignity (v. 29–31). These could have been included for completeness, but it is not an error that they are missing.; [minor] The father is given as "jake". The Hebrew name is "Jakeh" (יָקֶה). The ID "jake" is acceptable as a lowercase ID, but it should be verified that this is consistent with the rest of the database and that there is a profile with this ID.; [minor] The footnote about Agur's prayer uses the expression "an ideal of mediocrity". The word "mediocrity" has negative connotations in Norwegian. It would be better to use "the golden mean" or "an ideal of moderation".

versions.summary: Agur, son of Jake (Jakeh), is the author of Proverbs chapter 30. His identity and origin are debated – he may have been a non-Israelite wise man from Massa, an area linked to northwestern Arabia. The chapter opens with a deep and humble confession of human limitations before the Almighty God, followed by a strong affirmation of the reliability of God's word. Agur is especially known for his prayer for honesty and moderation – neither wealth nor poverty – and for his sharp numerical proverbs that draw insight from the world of nature. His text testifies to a reflective thinker who unites humility, reverence for God, and observation of creation in his search for wisdom.
versions.title: Author of Proverbs 30
versions.reason: [minor] Proverbs 30:19 mentions 'the way of a serpent over the rock/stone' – not 'the mountain'. But more importantly, the traditional translation is 'the way of a serpent on a rock'. This is a small nuance, but it can be noted. Otherwise, the content is correct.; [minor] Proverbs 30:29-31 refers to four things that move with dignity, but many textual witnesses also include verses 32-33 as a concluding exhortation. It may be considered to include these for completeness, but it is not strictly necessary since verses 29-31 cover the actual list.

footnotes.text: The name 'Agur' (אָגוּר) may mean 'collector' in Hebrew, which could point to his role as one who gathered words of wisdom. His father 'Jakeh' (יָקֶה) may mean 'obedient' or 'pious'.

The expression 'the man from Massa' (hammassa) in Proverbs 30:1 can be translated either as 'the utterance/message' or as a geographical reference to Massa, an area in northwestern Arabia linked to the descendants of Ishmael (Gen 25:14). If the latter is correct, Agur may have been a non-Israelite wise man, showing that biblical wisdom literature also included insights from other peoples.

The names 'Ithiel' and 'Ucal' in Proverbs 30:1 are debated. Some scholars interpret them as proper names of Agur's companions, while others read them as Hebrew phrases: 'God is with me' (Ithiel) and 'I am exhausted/can go no further' (Ucal), which would then emphasize Agur's humility before God.

The rhetorical questions in Proverbs 30:4 ('Who has ascended to heaven and come down again?') have clear parallels to Job 38 and Isaiah 40:12. Early Christian writers also saw in the question 'What is his son's name?' a prophetic allusion to God's Son.

Agur's prayer in Proverbs 30:7-9 is one of very few personal prayers in Proverbs. It expresses an ideal of moderation – neither wealth nor poverty – which has parallels in ancient wisdom thought and in Jesus' prayer 'Give us today our daily bread' (Matt 6:11).

The numerical proverbs in Proverbs 30 (the pattern 'three things... yes, four') are a well-known literary form in ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, also found in Ugaritic texts from Ras Shamra. This form is used to build tension toward the final and most important element in the list.

The rock hyrax (Hebrew: שָׁפָן, shafan) mentioned in Proverbs 30:26 is likely the rock hyrax (Procavia capensis), a small mammal that still lives in Israel's mountainous regions. The animal was admired for its ability to dwell in inaccessible cliffs, which was seen as a sign of wisdom despite its physical weakness.

Proverbs 30 is one of two additions to Solomon's collection of proverbs (the other being King Lemuel's words in chapter 31). The inclusion of these chapters in the Israelite wisdom canon suggests that the editors of Proverbs recognized wisdom insights regardless of the author's ethnic background—a remarkable feature of the biblical wisdom tradition.
